Five professional writers share how they use AI, where it disappoints them, and what they still insist on doing themselves  ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌
https://every.?ev_audience=free


WHAT WRITERS WHO USE AI WANT YOU TO KNOW https://every.?ev_audience=free


FIVE PROFESSIONAL WRITERS SHARE HOW THEY USE AI, WHERE IT DISAPPOINTS THEM, AND WHAT THEY STILL INSIST ON DOING THEMSELVES https://every.?ev_audience=free

by Laura Entis https://every.?ev_audience=free

Midjourney/Every illustration.

Last week we launched How We Write Now, a series about how writers are using AI, starting with Katie Parrott https://every.?ev_audience=free’s guide to Compound Writing https://every.?ev_audience=free—her framework for developing ideas, shaping drafts, and carrying what you learn into the next piece. This week, Laura Entis https://every.?ev_audience=free, who has been reckoning honestly with her own AI workflow, goes further: She interviewed five professional writers—including Every CEO Dan Shipper https://every.?ev_audience=free, designer Maggie Appleton, and New York Times alum Kevin Roose—about where they let AI in and where they draw the line. She found that there is no universal recipe: The same tool that helps one writer think more clearly makes another’s prose worse. Read on for five distinct, idiosyncratic workflows (including custom prompts) that make a case that writing with AI is a skill in its own right.—Kate Lee https://every.

----------
howdy, it’s Barsee again.

happy wednesday, AI family, and welcome back to AI Valley.

**here are the biggest things worth knowing today:**

* OpenAI says AI solved one of maths’ biggest problems

* AI researchers are starting to quit over ‘out-of-control’ AI fears

* Plus trending AI tools, posts, and resources

Let’s _dive_ into the Valley of AI…


----------

----------
#### **VOICES**

## [DNSMOS passed. Your model still missed the mark. Why?](https://www.voices.com/solutions/audio-quality-whitepaper?utm_source=ai-valley&utm_medium=newsletter&utm_campaign=client_audio-quality-whitepaper_2026)

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/05397386-3808-4780-9a49-4214dacc6938/Newsletter_white_paper__1___1_.png?t=1788961609)
Follow image link: (https://www.voices.com/solutions/audio-quality-whitepaper?utm_source=ai-valley&utm_medium=newsletter&utm_campaign=client_audio-quality-whitepaper_2026)
Caption: Courtesy: Voices

You ran DNSMOS on your training set, and the average score cleared your threshold. That's usually the moment teams stop asking questions—and the moment real problems start.

DNSMOS is a general perceptual quality proxy. It wasn't built for your specific model or task, so it can pass audio that quietly hurts training and fail audio that would have helped. The cost shows up later: wasted compute, blown timelines, or a model that underperforms in production for reasons nobody can trace back to the data.

Voices' CTO DJ Jalali, along with the team's senior audio and voice data engineers, built a four-step calibration framework to set model-specific quality thresholds instead of trusting the raw DNSMOS number. The new white paper walks through where DNSMOS breaks down and how Voices validates audio for custom datasets at scale.

[Download the White Paper →](https://www.voices.com/solutions/audio-quality-whitepaper?utm_source=ai-valley&utm_medium=newsletter&utm_campaign=client_audio-quality-whitepaper_2026)

~_*This is sponsored_~


----------

----------
#### **THROUGH THE VALLEY**

**1/ OpenAI says AI solved one of maths’ biggest problems** - OpenAI is [claiming](https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/) its unreleased AI model just solved Navier-Stokes, the 3rd most famous unsolved math problem in the world that’s been open for ~90 years. It's one of the 7 Millennium Prize Problems, with a $1 million bounty.

OpenAI threw ~10,000 AI agents at the problem at once, letting them work in groups, share ideas, run code and search a cached version of the internet. They found the solution after ~88 hours, then GPT-6 Astra spent another 17 hours formalizing and verifying it in Lean.

There’s some drama though. A mathematician who spent a year working on a related Navier-Stokes result (also with AI) [says](https://x.com/MaleManlpulator/status/2097195868772303006) OpenAI got access to his work, raced to finish the bigger problem and then pressured him to drop his co-author, who works at Anthropic.

And a pretty important caveat: the mathematician’s related result has been verified, but OpenAI hasn’t released its proof of the actual Millennium Prize Problem yet. So for now, we mostly have to take their word for it.

**2/ AI researchers are starting to quit over ‘out-of-control’ AI fears** - Jacob Coxon [resigned](https://x.com/hilbertspaess/status/2097476196791709843?s=20) from Anthropic after three years doing pretraining research at OpenAI and Anthropic, saying neither company is acting responsibly and they’re “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

Tweet:  (https://twitter.com/hilbertspaess/status/2097476196791709843?s=20)

His argument is basically that the people building these systems know how serious this could get. He says researchers privately talk about AI potentially killing everyone by the end of the decade, but the race keeps going anyway.

And other researchers are backing him up. Anthropic’s Alignment Science Lead Evan Hubinger said “[we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans](https://x.com/EvanHub/status/2097497037956891126?s=20)”, putting his own odds at 10%+ in the next decade. Another researcher who left Google DeepMind in June said Jacob is right and that thinking about how to stop this was “[literally my day job](https://x.com/Turn_Trout/status/2097557335732359491?s=20).”

Coxon is now calling for labs to slow down and coordinate, potentially even temporarily stopping improvements to model capabilities.

Pretty wild that “should we actually keep building this?” is becoming a real debate among the people building it.

----------
# TRENDING TOOLS

* [Meta Muse](https://muse.ai/?aymh_complete=1) - the personal agent that understands your goals and works 24/7 to get things done for you

* [ChatGPT Images 2.5](https://x.com/OpenAI/status/2097394956457623964?s=20) - faster, sharper, smarter, with better tools for creating whatever you can dream of

* [ChatGPT Work](https://x.com/ChatGPT/status/2097018264048251309?s=20) - can now pick up on what makes your writing sound like… _you_. Your favorite phrases. Your very specific sign-off. your capitalizations quirks

* [AlphaGenome Atlas](https://x.com/GoogleDeepMind/status/2097325048109384166?s=20) - an AI-powered searchable database mapping the predicted impact of all 9 billion possible single-letter DNA changes

* [Minara Harness](https://x.com/minara/status/2097413018510618899?s=20) - general financial intelligence for everyone. Start from ideas. Turn signals into execution. And handle coding tasks like any other agent

TO READ—OR NOT TO READ THE CODE? https://every.


AI IS READY TO RUN YOUR WORK IN THE DARK. DON'T LET IT TURN THE LIGHTS OUT IN YOUR HEAD, TOO. https://every.

by Kieran Klaassen https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVG8gUmVhZOKAlE9yIE5vdCB0byBSZWFkIHRoZSBDb2RlPyIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQ0NzAsInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL0BraWVyYW5fMTM1NSIsInBvc2l0aW9uIjo0fQ==

Midjourney/Every illustration.

Was this newsletter forwarded to you? Sign up https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVG8gUmVhZOKAlE9yIE5vdCB0byBSZWFkIHRoZSBDb2RlPyIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQ0NzAsInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL2FjY291bnQiLCJwb3NpdGlvbiI6NX0= to get it in your inbox.



----------------------------------------



I’m shipping more than I ever have, but I think my brain has gotten softer.

For the last year, I’ve hunted for the parts of coding that still needed me, then replaced myself with something that could do it, whether that’s a skill, a framework, a data source, or a step that routes work to the next agent. This is the essence of Compound Engineering https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVG8gUmVhZOKAlE9yIE5vdCB0byBSZWFkIHRoZSBDb2RlPyIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQ0NzAsInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL2d1aWRlcy9jb21wb3VuZC1lbmdpbmVlcmluZyIsInBvc2l0aW9uIjo2fQ==: Teach the system to work once, and it does that work forever. This is how I build Cora https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVG8gUmVhZOKAlE9yIE5vdCB0byBSZWFkIHRoZSBDb2RlPyIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQ0NzAsInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2NvcmEuY29tcHV0ZXIvIiwicG9zaXRpb24iOjd9, Every’s email assistant, and across my career, I believe it to be the best product and engineering work I have done.

But somewhere along the way, I found that I had lost a feeling. It used to be that learning itself was the reward. But my mind increasingly felt like a TikTok feed—full of short-lived hits of dopamine that left nothing behind.

I started to notice that although the work was improving, I wasn’t. My own mind was the part of the system I had forgotten to measure.

So I built another loop into my system—to fill the gaps in my understanding before they became blind spots in my judgment.


THE DARK FACTORY TURNS OUT THE LIGHT IN YOUR HEAD

When building a product, getting out of the AI’s way is usually the right move. It makes sense to route around yourself when you are the slowest part of the system. But if all you’re thinking about is the product, you’re neglecting your own development.

The “ https://every. factory https://every.” https://every. describes an ideal state for automation in manufacturing: lights off, nobody on the floor, machines running through the night. But the risk, when automating your own work, is turning out the light in your head, too.

Plenty of work should run in the dark. When we rebuilt part of Cora’s inbox, we noticed that the space between the rows was four pixels too small. It was simple to have an agent diagnose the bug, restore the spacing, write the tests, and open the pull request—the package of code changes ready for review. My understanding would not have changed the decision. But it was important to understand it anyway.

Plenty of work looks mechanical until you understand enough to see the decision hiding inside it. Those are the places where I want to keep the lights on.


READ THE CODE TO LEARN

Last year, I wrote about how I stopped reading every line of code https://every. during code review. That’s still true—I don’t read code to verify the work. The planning, testing, and review agents handle that better than I do. What’s changed is that recently, I’ve started reading the code again. Not to check the work, but to learn. If your only reason for opening a diff—the line-by-line view of what changed—is suspicion, reading harder will not fix your process.

Here’s an example of what I mean: Back in July, I asked /ce-explain—a command I built that explains a concept or change by tracing it through my own codebase—to walk me through how Cora turns a change in Gmail into something a customer sees: Gmail flags the change, Cora waits a moment so related changes can arrive together, then works through the batch message by message. That one pass replaced dozens of scattered details with a single picture I could hold in my head.

Two weeks later, that picture is what let me tell the difference between a fix that sounded right and one that actually was. A customer reported that Cora had permanently deleted emails he’d alr

#### **THROUGH THE VALLEY**

Tweet:  (https://twitter.com/merettm/status/2096630018495377464?s=20)

**OpenAI’s chief scientist wants everyone to slow down** - Jakub Pachocki wants the industry to stop treating max-speed scaling as the default. In an essay called “[An Alien Mind](https://openai.com/index/an-alien-mind),” he argues that today’s systems are grown more than designed: a product of huge optimization runs, not a mind anyone fully understands. That, for him, is the point. You cannot assume this kind of intelligence will inherit human principles on its own.

He dates the shift to mid-2023, when OpenAI’s RLSlow project first showed reasoning models could keep scaling. He now thinks that pace could continue into recursive self-improvement: AI doing more of the work of building better AI. Goal-following has improved. Value alignment (honesty, integrity, “love for humanity” when no one is watching) has not. [The Hugging Face incident](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-ahead/) is his example.

The awkward part is OpenAI also thinks it needs more powerful models to defend against more powerful models. Cybersecurity is the obvious example, and Pachocki says future agents could potentially bargain with, trick or even blackmail people while pursuing their own goals.

And then there’s the timing: [GPT-6 Astra](https://openai.com/index/gpt-6-astra/) just shipped with big jumps in coding, computer use, cyber and science. Pachocki says it’s better aligned than the last generation, and still not enough. His conclusion: no lab has solved alignment and monitoring well enough to keep flooring it. He wants voluntary slowdowns, mandated safety bars and eventually international coordination.

Hello, and happy Sunday. The models kept coming this week—Anthropic’s Fable 5.1 https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiQSBTcGxpdCBWZXJkaWN0IG9uIEZhYmxlIHZzLiBBc3RyYSIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQ0NjksInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL3ZpYmUtY2hlY2svZmFibGUtNS0xLXZpYmUtY2hlY2siLCJwb3NpdGlvbiI6NX0= on Tuesday, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra https://every. on Thursday—and Katie Parrott https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiQSBTcGxpdCBWZXJkaWN0IG9uIEZhYmxlIHZzLiBBc3RyYSIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQ0NjksInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL0BrYXRpZS5wYXJyb3R0MTIiLCJwb3NpdGlvbiI6N30= compared the two in a report from our end-of-week camp for paid subscribers, where the team came away split. Between the releases, we kicked off our How We Write Now series with her guide to Compound Writing, her system for writing with AI, adapted from Kieran Klaassen https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiQSBTcGxpdCBWZXJkaWN0IG9uIEZhYmxlIHZzLiBBc3RyYSIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQ0NjksInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL0BraWVyYW5fMTM1NSIsInBvc2l0aW9uIjo4fQ==’s Compound Engineering https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiQSBTcGxpdCBWZXJkaWN0IG9uIEZhYmxlIHZzLiBBc3RyYSIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQ0NjksInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL2d1aWRlcy9jb21wb3VuZC1lbmdpbmVlcmluZyIsInBvc2l0aW9uIjo5fQ==. ----------------------------------------


HOW WE WORK NOW

FABLE 5.1 VS. ASTRA: WHERE EACH CAME OUT AHEAD

A model can impress you with its output and still frustrate you as a collaborator. With Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra both launching this week, choosing between them means getting specific about what you want a model to do—and how you want to work with it.

At our latest subscriber-only camp, we compared the two mega-models’ work side by side. As Dan Shipper https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiQSBTcGxpdCBWZXJkaWN0IG9uIEZhYmxlIHZzLiBBc3RyYSIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQ0NjksInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL0BkYW5zaGlwcGVyIiwicG9zaXRpb24iOjEzfQ== noted, those comparisons help us articulate our standards for good work. A prettier app might lose to one that needs fewer clicks. A stronger draft might come from the model that’s harder to steer.

Here’s where each came out ahead:

 * We’re split on which one’s a better daily driver. Kieran Klaassen https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiQSBTcGxpdCBWZXJkaWN0IG9uIEZhYmxlIHZzLiBBc3RyYSIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQ0NjksInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL0BraWVyYW5fMTM1NSIsInBvc2l0aW9uIjoxNH0= preferred Fable: It was easier to build on its work without asking it to undo unwanted additions. However, I found that on writing tasks, Astra was much easier to steer through a back-and-forth, while Fable needed more context up front. We weren’t looking for the same kind of collaborator.
 * Fable apps needed fewer clicks. Senior editor Jack Cheng https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiQSBTcGxpdCBWZXJkaWN0IG9uIEZhYmxlIHZzLiBBc3RyYSIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQ0NjksInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL0BqYWNrY2hlbmciLCJwb3NpdGlvbiI6MTV9 asked both models for an app to digitize his handwritten journals. Fable’s let him hold a page up to his Mac’s camera, press the space bar, and turn to the next one. Astra’s had a warmer visual style, more buttons, and more decisions between Jack and a scanned page. Dan preferred Fable’s simpler approach.
 * Fable got the diagram right. In anticipation, we’re republishing his April piece https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVGhlIEZvbGRlciBJcyB0aGUgQWdlbnQiLCJwb3N0X2lkIjo0NDY4LCJwb3N0X3R5cGUiOiJwb3N0IiwidXJsIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9ldmVyeS50by9zb3VyY2UtY29kZS90aGUtZm9sZGVyLWlzLXRoZS1hZ2VudCIsInBvc2l0aW9uIjo3fQ== on the folder-as-agent approach that let him orchestrate 44 specialized agents sustainably. ----------------------------------------



I spent three months trying to make agent swarms https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVGhlIEZvbGRlciBJcyB0aGUgQWdlbnQiLCJwb3N0X2lkIjo0NDY4LCJwb3N0X3R5cGUiOiJwb3N0IiwidXJsIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9jaGF0Z3B0LmNvbS9zaGFyZS9lLzY5ZGNlZDY4LWY2YmMtODAwZS1iNGM1LWFmNmExMzRkNDczNyIsInBvc2l0aW9uIjoxMn0= work.

The idea of multiplying myself by coordinating multiple agents at the same time was a compelling pitch as the sole engineer building Every’s AI email assistant, Cora https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVGhlIEZvbGRlciBJcyB0aGUgQWdlbnQiLCJwb3N0X2lkIjo0NDY4LCJwb3N0X3R5cGUiOiJwb3N0IiwidXJsIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9jb3JhLmNvbXB1dGVyIiwicG9zaXRpb24iOjEzfQ==. If I could summon a fleet of AI agents https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVGhlIEZvbGRlciBJcyB0aGUgQWdlbnQiLCJwb3N0X2lkIjo0NDY4LCJwb3N0X3R5cGUiOiJwb3N0IiwidXJsIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9ldmVyeS50by9ndWlkZXMvYWdlbnQtbmF0aXZlIiwicG9zaXRpb24iOjE0fQ==, let them coordinate, and watch them produce work no single agent could match, it would relieve some of my overwhelm.

I tried everything to make it work—Claude Code https://every. teams, agents dispatching tasks to other agents, orchestration setups https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVGhlIEZvbGRlciBJcyB0aGUgQWdlbnQiLCJwb3N0X2lkIjo0NDY4LCJwb3N0X3R5cGUiOiJwb3N0IiwidXJsIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9ldmVyeS50by9zb3VyY2UtY29kZS90aGUtdGhyZWUtd2F5cy1pLXdvcmstd2l0aC1sbG1zIiwicG9zaXRpb24iOjE2fQ== wh

ere a lead agent managed a pool of workers. Many iterations, many burned tokens.

But more agents didn’t make me faster. I’ve run parallel Claude Code sessions https://every. for months, which works when each agent has a clear task, and I’m directing the work. The swarm experiment was different: agents coordinating with each other, deciding what to work on, producing output I hadn’t shaped. When 10 of them finished simultaneously, I had 10 results to evaluate https://every. without enough context to know which ones I could trust. AI agents don’t have a speed limit, but the person managing them still does.

I kept looking for a smarter orchestration layer—a better protocol or a tighter framework that would filter the output and tell me which result to trus
